To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Turkey and Bulgaria, two countries that are in close geographic proximity, have a similar industrial structure and are in the same stage of development, are in fact very different in terms of the value-added they retain from their exports and in terms of the upgrading of their local firms.

(1) Turkey retains higher value-added for the local economy than Bulgaria, although the exports are concentrated in down-market segments at the beginning of our period of analysis, and (2) firms in Turkey have better performance than firms in Bulgaria at the end of our period of research.

(a) Turkey retains higher value-added for the local economy; (b) firms in Turkey are better positioned compared to firms in Turkey at the end of the period of research; (c) the results show higher upgrading at product, process, organizational and functional level for firms in Turkey; (d) firms in Bulgaria are more dependent on foreign suppliers, trade agents, and concentration in the top market; (e) lock-in into low value-added segments of the GVS is difficult to overcome
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: what is the impact of internationalization and GVCs on local upgrading and dependency of firms in Bulgaria and Turkey?

the following: (1) the role of internationalization in the upgrading of firms in Bulgaria and Turkey; (2) the role of state and business actors in the upgrading process; (3) the impact of the GVC framework on our understanding of industrial upgrading in Bulgaria and Turkey.

how we can study and how we can explain the industrial upgrading of the host economy, and how the GVC analytical framework and its methodology can be applied in other countries, in other sectors, and in other market regions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GVC approach is useful in explaining and analyzing the industrial and firm upgrading of the textile and apparel sector in Turkey and Bulgaria.
Turkey has been more successful than Bulgaria in upgrading its textile and apparel firms, but that both countries have been less successful than other developing countries in the same sector.
the GVC framework is a powerful tool for understanding industrial and firm upgrading, but it should be complemented with other tools and methodologies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the internationalization of firms from Turkey and Bulgaria in the textile and apparel sector has resulted in a low-value added, and that the local firms are locked into low-value added niches of the GVC.
the GVC framework is a useful tool to study industrial upgrading in developing countries, but it should be complemented with other analytical approaches.

we have found that local upgrading in Turkey and Bulgaria has been limited to a few firms in Turkey, while most Bulgarian firms have been locked-in to low value-added segments of the GVs, and that local firms in both countries have been locked out of the GVC.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the local upgrading of the textile and apparel firms in the two host economies is constrained by the lock-in into the low-value added niches and by the lack of institutional support for the local upgrading.
the GVC’s approach is a useful tool for analyzing the upgrading of firms in the host economy.

the GVC framework, which is based primarily on quantitative methods, should be complemented by qualitative methods, such as interviews and surveys, to better understand the local upgrading process and to explain it.
